# **Dynamic Causality and Structural Identification in Multivariate Time Series: From Predictive Precedence to Structural Identification**

## **Foundations of Multivariate Dynamic Modeling**

Filler check

The quantitative analysis of joint economic and physical processes over time requires a mathematical framework capable of capturing complex temporal dependencies.1 Christopher Sims introduced the Vector Autoregressive (VAR) model as a flexible multivariate alternative to traditional simultaneous equation systems, which relied on arbitrary classifications of endogenous and exogenous variables.3 A standard reduced-form ![][image1]\-dimensional VAR model of order ![][image2], denoted as VAR(![][image2]), expresses a vector of ![][image1] stationary time series variables, ![][image3], as a linear function of their own past values and a vector of white noise disturbances 1:  
![][image4]  
In this formulation, ![][image5] is a ![][image6] vector of intercept terms, ![][image7] represent ![][image8] coefficient matrices for each lag ![][image9], and ![][image10] is a ![][image6] vector of unobservable, serially uncorrelated white noise innovations with a symmetric, positive-definite covariance matrix ![][image11].1 The covariance matrix ![][image11] contains the variances of the individual equations on its diagonal and the contemporaneous covariances of the errors on its off-diagonal elements.6 Because every variable in the system is regressed on the identical set of lagged regressors, the parameters of each equation can be estimated independently and consistently using Ordinary Least Squares (OLS).1  
To illustrate this structural setup in an empirical context, consider a trivariate VAR(1) system modeling clinical patient dynamics with variables representing Heart Rate (![][image12]), Respiratory Rate (![][image13]), and Oxygen Saturation (![][image14]) 1:  
![][image15]  
![][image16]  
![][image17]  
This scalar formulation highlights how each clinical variable in the system is regressed on the identical set of lagged regressors, allowing the parameters of each equation to be estimated independently.1  
The empirical validity of a VAR model depends on verifying covariance stationarity and selecting the optimal lag length ![][image2].1 Covariance stationarity requires that the first two moments of the stochastic process—the mean and the autocovariances—are finite and time-invariant.7 If a VAR is estimated on non-stationary variables, the resulting standard error estimates are biased, and any subsequent statistical inferences are highly suspect.1 To establish stationarity, researchers rely on a combination of visual inspections of time-series plots and formal statistical procedures, primarily the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) and the Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin (KPSS) tests.1 When a series exhibits a unit root, differencing the data is necessary to achieve stationarity before integration into a standard VAR framework.1  
Another challenge in real-world causal discovery is the presence of missing values and irregular sampling intervals, which violate the uniform sampling assumption of linear VAR models.11 To address this difficulty, researchers deploy a two-stage system wherein missing data entries are reconstructed using Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) to yield an evenly sampled time series prior to performing causal parameter estimation.11  
Once stationarity is established, the lag length ![][image2] must be determined to balance the trade-off between model parsimony and misspecification bias.1 Incorporating too few lags omits vital historical information, resulting in serially correlated residuals and biased parameter estimates.1 Conversely, including excessive lags overparameterizes the system, inflating the standard errors of the coefficient estimates and reducing the model's out-of-sample forecasting performance.1 The optimal lag order is typically identified by minimizing multivariate information criteria evaluated over a designated range of candidate lags, ![][image18].1

| Information Criterion | Mathematical Formulation | Consistency Asymptotics | Finite-Sample Performance |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)** | **![][image19]** | Inconsistent; asymptotically overestimates the true lag order with positive probability.14 | Minimizes mean-square forecast errors; performs well in avoiding underfitting.1 |
| **Schwarz Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC / SBIC)** | **![][image20]** | Strongly consistent; the probability of selecting the true lag order approaches one as ![][image21].14 | Highly parsimonious; prone to underestimating the true lag length in small samples.12 |
| **Hannan-Quinn Information Criterion (HQIC)** | **![][image22]** | Strongly consistent for multivariate processes with dimension ![][image23].14 | Serves as a compromise; more restrictive than AIC for samples where ![][image24].14 |

In these mathematical formulations, ![][image25] represents the estimated covariance matrix of the residuals from a VAR of order ![][image2], ![][image1] is the number of endogenous variables, ![][image26] is the active sample size, and ![][image27] denotes the matrix determinant.13 While AIC is often favored for forecasting purposes due to its aversion to underfitting, BIC and HQIC are preferred for structural analysis where identifying the exact data-generating process is paramount.1

## **Granger Causality: Predictive Precedence, Multiple Testing, and Modern Alternatives**

The concept of Granger causality addresses the dynamic, predictive relationships between variables within a multivariate system.9 Grounded in the temporal axiom that a cause must precede its effect and contain unique information about that effect, Clive Granger defined the relationship probabilistically.15 Let ![][image28] represent the set of all available information in the universe up to time ![][image29], and let ![][image30] denote a modified information set excluding the history of the time series ![][image31].15 A stationary process ![][image31] is said to Granger-cause another stationary process ![][image32] if the conditional probability distribution of ![][image33] given ![][image28] differs from the conditional distribution of ![][image33] given ![][image30] 15:  
![][image34]  
where ![][image35] represents an arbitrary non-empty Borel set.15 In empirical applications, this definition is operationalized through linear regression models where the information sets are restricted to the histories of the observed variables.15  
To test the null hypothesis that a stationary series ![][image31] does not Granger-cause another stationary series ![][image32], an analyst compares two linear specifications.9 The restricted (univariate) autoregression models ![][image36] solely as a function of its own historical values 9:  
![][image37]  
The unrestricted (augmented) autoregression incorporates the historical values of both ![][image32] and ![][image31] 9:  
![][image38]  
The lag lengths ![][image39] and ![][image40] are chosen to eliminate serial correlation in the residuals.10 The null hypothesis of non-causality corresponds to the linear restriction:  
![][image41]  
This hypothesis is formally evaluated using a Wald or joint ![][image42]\-test.9 If the joint explanatory power of the lagged values of ![][image31] is statistically significant, the null hypothesis is rejected, and it is concluded that ![][image31] Granger-causes ![][image32].9 In a multivariate VAR setting, a variable ![][image43] Granger-causes ![][image44] if any of the coefficients on the lagged values of ![][image43] in the equation for ![][image44] are statistically different from zero.15 Alternatively, researchers execute leave-one-out, exclude-all, or block-wise Granger causality tests to assess the joint influence of subsets of variables, utilizing family-wise error rate corrections like the Bonferroni adjustment (![][image45]) to control the inflated false discovery rate that accompanies simultaneous hypothesis testing.17  
Granger causality has several significant limitations.15 First, it measures "predictive precedence" rather than physical, manipulative, or philosophical causality.9 Granger himself later characterized the relationship as "temporally related" to distance it from philosophical notions of causation.15  
The bivariate test is highly susceptible to omitted variable bias.15 If a latent third process ![][image46] drives both ![][image31] and ![][image32] with different temporal lags, the bivariate test will falsely indicate that ![][image31] Granger-causes ![][image32].15 Bivariate systems also fail to capture non-linear causal dynamics or interactions occurring in higher-order moments, such as conditional variance.15 Additionally, if the sampling interval is too wide relative to the speed of the underlying process, the causal mechanism is obscured; conversely, oversampling can introduce noise or spurious feedback patterns.15  
To scale Granger causality to high-dimensional systems (where the number of variables ![][image47] approaches or exceeds the sample size ![][image26]), modern methodologies utilize sparse VAR frameworks.19 In these settings, the Granger-causal network is represented as a directed graph ![][image48], where vertices ![][image49] correspond to time series and a directed edge ![][image50] exists if and only if at least one lag coefficient ![][image51].19  
Causal discovery in high-dimensional networks is formulated as a multiple testing problem across the sequence of hypotheses ![][image52].19 To control the False Discovery Rate (FDR) and directional FDR (dFDR) while maintaining statistical power, researchers apply high-dimensional inference procedures.19 One prominent approach utilizes a debiased Lasso estimator to obtain asymptotically normal ![][image29]\-statistics for individual lag parameters.19  
Another procedure employs asymptotic e-variables (the e-BH procedure) to construct robust multiple testing routines that are invariant to complex cross-sectional dependence structures within the high-dimensional error matrix.19

When linear autoregressive assumptions are violated, standard F-tests fail.15 To detect causality in higher-order moments, such as variance, non-parametric tests are deployed as diagnostic tools to guide the construction of non-linear parametric models.15  
Furthermore, machine learning paradigms offer alternative frameworks to identify non-linear predictive precedence without specifying explicit functional forms.20 One such framework reformulates Granger causality as a supervised ternary classification problem, assigning labels representing forward directionality (![][image53]), feedback (![][image54]), or non-causality.21 To represent the underlying distributions, this method maps the conditional probability distributions ![][image55] and ![][image56] into a reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) using kernel mean embeddings, subsequently measuring the distance between them via the Maximum Mean Discrepancy (MMD) to determine the causal label.21  
For larger systems, Deep Learning-based Group Causal Inference models complex non-linear structures using architectures like DeepAR.20 This methodology identifies causal directionality across groups of variables by training deep neural networks and performing group-level interventions, evaluating model invariance to determine if the distribution of output residuals remains stable across interventional environments.20

## **Cointegration and Error Correction: Modeling Long-Run Equilibrium Systems**

Many macroeconomic and financial time series are non-stationary and integrated of order one, ![][image57], meaning they accumulate past shocks and exhibit a stochastic trend.7 Regressing an ![][image57] variable on another independent ![][image57] variable yields a "spurious regression" characterized by an inflated ![][image58] and highly significant ![][image29]\-statistics, despite the absence of any true economic relationship.8 To resolve this, variables must be differenced to ![][image59].8 However, differencing eliminates long-run level information, restricting the model to short-run dynamic associations.8  
Cointegration provides a mathematical bridge between short-run dynamics and long-run equilibrium.23 Two or more ![][image57] series are cointegrated if there exists a linear combination of them that is stationary, ![][image59].7 Structurally, this implies that while the individual variables drift apart in the short run due to temporary shocks, they are bound together in the long run by a stable equilibrium attractor.23 Mathematically, if ![][image36] is a ![][image6] vector of ![][image57] variables, they are cointegrated if there exists a vector ![][image60] such that 7:  
![][image61]  
where ![][image60] is the cointegrating vector.7 For a system of ![][image1] variables, there can exist at most ![][image62] linearly independent cointegrating vectors.7 In economic modeling, this requires the equations to "balance"; the order of integration on the left side of an equation must match the order of integration on the right side.7 It is mathematically impossible for an ![][image57] variable to be equal to a stationary ![][image59] variable without a cointegrating relationship to balance the stochastic trend.7  
The estimation and testing of cointegrating relationships are primarily conducted via two paradigms: the Engle-Granger two-step method and the Johansen maximum likelihood framework.8  
The Engle-Granger procedure is a residual-based approach designed for a single cointegrating relationship (![][image63]).25 In the first step, the static long-run relationship is estimated using OLS on the levels of the variables 25:  
![][image64]  
The estimated residuals ![][image65] are then extracted.25 In the second step, an ADF test is performed on these residuals to determine if they contain a unit root.25 Because the OLS estimation minimizes the residual variance, the generated residuals are mathematically guaranteed to be as stationary as possible, which biases the standard Dickey-Fuller critical values downward.25 Consequently, the test must employ non-standard Phillips-Ouliaris (PO) critical values, which depend on the number of regressors and the deterministic trend specifications.25 If the residuals are stationary, the null of no cointegration is rejected, and an Error Correction Model (ECM) is estimated 29:  
![][image66]  
The parameter ![][image67] represents the speed of adjustment, reflecting the proportion of disequilibrium corrected in each subsequent period.25  
The Johansen maximum likelihood test generalizes cointegration analysis to multivariate systems by allowing for multiple cointegrating vectors (![][image68]).26 Johansen's methodology reformulates a general VAR(![][image2]) model into a Vector Error Correction Model (VECM) 23:  
![][image69]  
where ![][image36] is a ![][image6] vector of ![][image57] series, ![][image70] captures the short-run transitory dynamics, and ![][image71] is the long-run impact matrix defined as 23:  
![][image72]  
The cointegration properties of the system are determined by the rank of the matrix ![][image71], denoted as ![][image73].23 There are three structural possibilities:

1. If ![][image74], the matrix ![][image71] is the null matrix, implying that there are no cointegrating relationships.24 In this case, the VECM simplifies to a VAR in first differences.26  
2. If ![][image75], the matrix has full rank, indicating that all individual variables in ![][image36] are already stationary, ![][image59], rendering cointegration analysis irrelevant.24  
3. If ![][image76], there exist ![][image77] independent cointegrating vectors.24 The matrix ![][image71] can be decomposed as ![][image78], where ![][image60] is a ![][image79] matrix of cointegrating parameters (representing the long-run relations) and ![][image67] is a ![][image79] matrix of adjustment coefficients (representing the speed of adjustment toward the equilibrium).23

| Specification Dimension | Engle-Granger Two-Step Method | Johansen Maximum Likelihood Test |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Statistical Basis** | Single-equation OLS residual-based unit root testing.25 | System-wide maximum likelihood estimation of a VECM.23 |
| **Capacity for Cointegration Vectors** | Limited to identifying a maximum of one (![][image63]) cointegrating vector.27 | Capable of discovering multiple (![][image80]) cointegrating vectors.7 |
| **Sensitivity to Variable Ordering** | Highly sensitive; changing the left-hand dependent variable alters the test residuals.24 | Perfectly invariant; treats all variables as endogenously determined within a system.24 |
| **Error Propagation & Statistical Power** | High risk of error propagation; biases in the first-stage OLS contaminate the second-stage ECM.8 | Higher overall statistical power; estimates all parameters simultaneously.26 |
| **Distributional Properties** | Residuals follow non-standard Phillips-Ouliaris (PO) distributions.25 | Statistics follow non-standard multivariate distributions based on Brownian motion.25 |

The testing proceeds sequentially starting from ![][image87].26 The first non-rejection of the null hypothesis provides the estimate of the cointegration rank ![][image77].27  
Because the critical values of these tests are highly sensitive to the inclusion of deterministic components (constants and linear trends), researchers apply the Pantula Principle.23 This principle systematically guides model selection by testing joint hypotheses concerning both the rank ![][image77] and the deterministic trends across five nested specifications (ranging from no constant or trend to a quadratic trend), proceeding from the most restrictive model to the least restrictive.23

When interpreting cointegrating systems, a frequent conflict arises between the pre-testing phase (univariate ADF unit root tests) and the post-testing phase (restriction tests on the cointegrating space).32 While pre-testing classifies variables individually as ![][image57] or ![][image59], the multivariate Johansen post-test evaluates whether specific unit vectors are contained within the cointegrating space.32  
Because stationarity of a component variable is the null hypothesis of the post-test restriction, a variable classified as ![][image57] in pre-testing may have its unit vector accepted as cointegrating in post-testing, indicating stationarity.32 To resolve these contradictions, econometricians rely on modified unit root tests that incorporate the other variables in the system, rather than strictly univariate tests, to align pre- and post-estimation inferences.32

## **Robust Causal Testing under Non-Stationarity: The Toda-Yamamoto Procedure**

When time series are non-stationary, standard Granger causality testing estimated on levels exhibits non-standard asymptotic distributions.33 Specifically, Sims, Stock, and Watson demonstrated that the Wald test statistic for joint coefficient exclusions does not follow a standard asymptotic ![][image97] distribution if the variables are integrated or cointegrated.33 This distribution failure occurs because the test cannot be written entirely as a transformation of stationary differences, leaving a non-stationary level term that distorts the test's critical values.33  
To demonstrate the algebra of this failure, consider a bivariate system where we test if ![][image98] Granger-causes ![][image99]. Under the null, the lag polynomial of ![][image98] is restricted.33 By sequentially substituting level terms with differences:  
![][image100]  
we can rewrite the lag polynomial as a sum of differences plus a single lagged level term 33:  
![][image101]  
While the differenced terms ![][image102] are stationary, the final level term ![][image103] remains non-stationary if the underlying process is ![][image57].33 Any joint exclusion test on the original coefficients ![][image104] necessarily tests this non-stationary level term, preventing the Wald statistic from converging to a standard ![][image97] distribution and leading to severe size distortions and spurious causality.16  
To circumvent this, Toda and Yamamoto (1995), along with Dolado and Lütkepohl (1996), proposed a robust procedure that allows for Granger causality testing within a levels VAR framework, completely bypassing the need for pre-testing for cointegration or unit roots.34  
The implementation of the Toda-Yamamoto procedure unfolds in a systematic sequence of mathematical and diagnostic steps.10  
First, the analyst determines the maximum order of integration, ![][image105], suspecting to exist among the variables in the system using standard unit root tests (ADF, KPSS).10 For instance, if the system contains a mixture of ![][image59] and ![][image57] variables, ![][image106]; if an ![][image107] variable is present, ![][image108].10  
Second, the optimal lag length ![][image109] for a VAR in levels is selected using standard information criteria (AIC, BIC, HQIC) and verified using diagnostic tests to ensure that the residuals are free from serial correlation.10 The condition ![][image110] must be satisfied.34  
Third, the analyst estimates an intentionally overparameterized VAR in levels of order ![][image111] 34:  
![][image112]  
Fourth, a Wald test is performed to evaluate linear restrictions on the coefficients of the first ![][image109] lags.10 Crucially, the coefficients of the extra ![][image105] lagged vectors are ignored during the restriction test.10 For a bivariate system where ![][image113], testing whether ![][image114] Granger-causes ![][image115] involves evaluating the restriction:  
![][image116]  
where ![][image117] are the coefficients of ![][image118] in the ![][image99] equation. Because the model has been augmented with ![][image105] extra lags, the Wald test statistic asymptotically follows a standard ![][image97] distribution with ![][image109] degrees of freedom.10 The inclusion of these redundant, unconstrained lags fixes the asymptotic properties of the estimator by ensuring that the test on the first ![][image109] parameters is equivalent to a test on stationary differences, preserving standard asymptotic properties regardless of whether the series are ![][image59], ![][image57], or cointegrated.33  
Despite its robustness to pre-testing bias, the Toda-Yamamoto (TY) procedure exhibits a significant "blind spot" in specific econometric environments.33 When variables are cointegrated, the long-run causal transmission occurs primarily through the levels (the cointegrating vector) rather than through short-run differences.33 Because the TY procedure adds an extra, untested ![][image105] lag to the regression, this augmenting lag acts as a powerful proxy for the omitted long-run level relationships.33  
Asymptotically, the level term exhibits zero correlation with future differences, meaning the augmenting lag absorbs the long-run causality.33 Consequently, the Wald test conducted on only the first ![][image109] lags fails to reject the null hypothesis of non-causality, even when a potent causal relationship exists through the cointegrating vector.33 In finite samples, this can lead to a severe loss of power (Type II error).33 For example, simulations demonstrate that in cointegrated systems with sample sizes around 500 observations, the TY procedure may reject a false null of non-causality only 10% of the time, whereas standard Granger tests on cointegrated levels reject it 80% of the time.33

## **Contemporaneous Interactions and Causal Discovery in Time Series**

Standard reduced-form VAR and Granger causality models are strictly lagged structures; they assume that causal influences require time to propagate and thus cannot model contemporaneous relationships within the same sampling interval.6 This is reflected in the covariance matrix ![][image11] of the reduced-form innovations ![][image10], where non-zero off-diagonal elements indicate contemporaneous correlations but remain silent on the direction of causality.6  
To model instantaneous causal mechanisms, economists utilize Structural Vector Autoregressions (SVAR).3 A linear SVAR(![][image2]) model is expressed as 3:  
![][image119]  
where ![][image120] is a ![][image8] matrix that directly governs the contemporaneous relationships among the variables in ![][image36], and ![][image121] is a ![][image6] vector of structural shocks assumed to be mutually orthogonal (diagonal covariance matrix ![][image122]).3 The relationship between the observable reduced-form innovations ![][image10] and the unobservable structural shocks ![][image121] is given by 6:  
![][image123]  
To estimate the parameters in ![][image120], the model must be identified.3 Because the symmetric reduced-form covariance matrix ![][image124] contains only ![][image125] unique parameters, and the structural system contains ![][image126] parameters in ![][image120] (excluding diagonal normalization), a minimum of ![][image127] restrictions must be imposed on ![][image120] to achieve exact identification.3  
Historically, this was achieved via a Cholesky decomposition, forcing ![][image120] to be lower triangular, which assumes a recursive, asymmetric causal order.6 Alternatively, modern SVAR models impose short-run restrictions (zero constraints on ![][image120]), long-run restrictions (zero constraints on the cumulative impact matrix), or sign restrictions (constraining the direction of impulse responses) motivated by macroeconomic theory.3  
To avoid relying on subjective theoretical restrictions, computer scientists have developed data-driven causal discovery algorithms designed for time series.18 These algorithms treat the identification of ![][image120] as a problem of learning a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) from observational data.41 Under the assumption of continuous additive noise, if contemporaneous relationships are non-linear, the underlying causal DAG is uniquely identifiable from the observational distribution without any prior theoretical restrictions.41 Similarly, if the structural errors ![][image121] are non-Gaussian, Independent Component Analysis (ICA) can be used to uniquely identify the ![][image120] matrix.41  
Furthermore, under the assumption of equal noise variances, researchers utilize procedures like ENVAR to search over the induced observational equivalence class for a sparse, normalized structural representative, resolving the typical non-identifiability of linear Gaussian systems.39  
In scientific domains where physical mechanisms are well-understood, the SVAR-FM (Structural VAR with Flow Matching) framework combines continuous distribution learners with physical simulators.42 Treating the simulator as a mechanical realization of Judea Pearl's do-operator (![][image128]), clamping variables within the simulation physically severs confounding paths.42  
This allows the researcher to estimate a non-linear structural assignment 42:  
![][image129]  
where ![][image130] and ![][image131] denote the contemporaneous and lagged parent variables, respectively, and ![][image132] is a non-linear causal mechanism learned via conditional flow matching.42 This simulation-based interventional data resolves the observational non-identifiability of the structural VAR.42  
To extend these concepts to partially observed systems, algorithms such as SVAR-FCI and SVAR-GFCI integrate latent components into the dynamical model, permitting robust structural identification even in the presence of unobserved confounders.43  
In high-dimensional, highly autocorrelated time-series settings where classical VAR structures fail due to the curse of dimensionality, the PCMCI (Peter and Clark Momentary Conditional Independence) algorithm represents a state-of-the-art causal discovery framework.18 PCMCI addresses two primary challenges: controlling false positives driven by autocorrelation and maintaining statistical power in high dimensions.18 The algorithm splits causal discovery into two distinct phases.18  
The first phase, the Condition-Selection Phase (PC1), is executed.18 For each variable ![][image133] in the system, a modified, highly accelerated version of the PC skeleton search is run to identify a conditioning set of candidate parents, ![][image134], from the past.18 This is achieved by iteratively testing conditional independence using partial correlation or mutual information and removing lagged variables that do not share a statistically significant association.18 This step reduces the dimensionality of the search space.40  
The second phase, the Momentary Conditional Independence (MCI) Test Phase, is performed.18 To test whether a lagged variable ![][image135] causally influences ![][image36], PCMCI evaluates the momentary conditional independence 40:  
![][image136]  
By conditioning not only on the parents of the target variable ![][image36] but also on the parents of the historical driver ![][image135], the MCI test resolves a major issue in time-series causal inference: it neutralizes the confounding effect of autocorrelation in both series and accounts for lagged common confounders.40 This two-step process yields well-calibrated ![][image2]\-values and severely mitigates the false-positive rate.40  
However, PCMCI is highly vulnerable to subsampling bias.18 Causal interactions in physical and economic systems frequently occur at a much higher temporal resolution than the rate at which data is observed or sampled.18 When the sampling interval is too wide (e.g., observing a process daily when causal exchanges occur hourly), the true time-lagged causal links are lost, and the system appears to exhibit instantaneous contemporaneous feedback.18 This loss of temporal precedence severely degrades the condition-selection phase, resulting in missing links, spurious contemporaneous edges, and an overall distortion of the learned causal graph.18

## **Synthesis and Comparative Evaluation of Causal Time Series Methodologies**

To systematically guide researchers in selecting the appropriate causal inference framework, the table below provides a structured comparative analysis of the methodologies examined in this report, classifying them across key structural, statistical, and computational dimensions.1

| Methodology | Data Requirements | Primary Identification Mechanism | Capacity for Cointegration | Major Limitations |
| :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **Reduced-Form VAR** 1 | Stationary ![][image59] time series.1 | Joint linear prediction via Ordinary Least Squares.1 | None (requires pre-differencing).1 | Omits contemporaneous causality and non-linear interactions.6 |
| **Bivariate Granger** 9 | Stationary ![][image59] time series.9 | Linear lag exclusion testing (![][image42]\-test / Wald test).9 | None (requires pre-differencing).9 | Susceptible to omitted variable bias and sampling rates.15 |
| **Johansen VECM** 27 | Non-stationary ![][image57] series.27 | Maximum likelihood rank estimation of ![][image71] matrix.26 | High (estimates up to ![][image62] vectors).7 | Sensitive to lag length and deterministic trend assumptions.29 |
| **Toda-Yamamoto** 34 | Mixed integration orders ![][image137] levels.34 | Augmented levels VAR(![][image138]) Wald test.10 | Robust (invariant to cointegration).34 | Severe power loss (Type II error) in cointegrated systems.33 |
| **SVAR** 3 | Stationary ![][image59] time series.6 | Contemporaneous restrictions (![][image120]), non-Gaussianity, or ICA.3 | Requires VECM formulation.27 | Relies on potentially subjective theoretical assumptions.6 |
| **PCMCI** 40 | High-dimensional stationary series.40 | Conditioning on parent sets (![][image139]) \+ MCI test.40 | None (assumes stationary SCM).40 | Vulnerable to subsampling and latent confounders.18 |
| **SVAR-FM** 42 | Level series with physical simulator.42 | Simulation-clamped interventional flow matching.42 | None (handled via simulator).42 | Computationally intensive; requires a functional simulator.42 |

Navigating causal inference in multivariate time series requires matching the specific econometric or computational methodology to the structural properties of the observed data.1 Standard VAR and Granger causality models offer a robust foundation for predicting stationary series, but they fail to capture true physical interventions and are highly sensitive to omitted variables.1 When variables are non-stationary, cointegration techniques like the Engle-Granger and Johansen VECM systems preserve long-run level dynamics while preventing spurious regressions.8 In the presence of uncertain integration orders, the Toda-Yamamoto procedure provides a statistically robust alternative, though it exhibits a severe power blind spot when causal transmission is primarily long-run.33 Finally, for contemporaneous and high-dimensional systems, Structural VARs and causal discovery algorithms like PCMCI offer mathematical pathways to identify direct causal structures, provided analysts account for the distorting effects of subsampling and non-stationarity.6
